Answers and explanations
  1. privilege review Turn 2. Privilege review is the assessment stage; it does not mean the protection has already been established.
  2. status Turn 4. Status identifies the document's actual workflow stage, preventing collection or review from being mistaken for completed disclosure.
  3. email thread Turn 6. The complete email thread supplies context for the different messages; a single isolated line may not support accurate classification.
  4. Responsiveness Turn 8. Responsiveness concerns the scope of a request, not whether a legal protection may apply; changing that label would hide a separate question.
  5. redaction Turn 10. A redaction masks approved content in a disclosure copy; it is not permission to change the preserved original or redact without authorization.
  6. metadata Turn 12. Metadata contains file attributes that may support review context; retaining only visible text can omit important information.
  7. Bates number Turn 14. A Bates number identifies pages in a legal document sequence; inventing one could misleadingly imply an assigned production reference.
  8. privilege log Turn 16. A privilege log describes withheld material according to governing requirements; its contents need review and should not reveal the claimed protected substance.
  9. clawback Turn 18. A clawback mechanism may address inadvertent disclosure under applicable arrangements, but it does not justify bypassing the required review.
  10. handoff Turn 20. A handoff transfers the item, context, unresolved question, and responsibility; those details allow counsel to decide without guessing the workflow history.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Requesting review of a potentially privileged chain

The lesson's email chain is in a review set, not a production set, and privilege is unconfirmed.

  1. Document reviewer: Could you review this email chain for potential privilege before any production decision?
  2. Review lawyer: Where is it currently located, and has it been included in a production set?
  3. Document reviewer: It is in the review set only. I haven't determined whether privilege applies.
  4. Review lawyer: Good. Keep that distinction explicit instead of describing it as a disclosure incident.
  5. Document reviewer: I'll provide the review reference and explain which passages prompted the concern.
  6. Review lawyer: Use the restricted review system rather than copying the chain into general messages.
  7. Document reviewer: Should I label it privileged or work product now to resolve the queue?
  8. Review lawyer: Flag it for assessment; those determinations require review in the relevant context.
  9. Document reviewer: Please confirm when you can assess it before the production decision is taken.
  10. Review lawyer: I'll confirm the review slot and record the determination through the discovery workflow.
Requesting a missing attachment for discovery review

Separate fictional discovery exercise: a review email refers to an attachment absent from the collected set; its contents are unknown.

  1. Discovery lawyer: Could you check the collection record for the attachment referenced in this email?
  2. ESI coordinator: Yes. Do you want a collection-status check, or are you assuming it was intentionally withheld?
  3. Discovery lawyer: Only a status check. We don't know why the attachment is absent.
  4. ESI coordinator: I'll trace the item reference without describing the missing contents as established evidence.
  5. Discovery lawyer: Please confirm what can be located before we finish assessing the email's context.
  6. ESI coordinator: If I find a matching file, should it move straight into production?
  7. Discovery lawyer: No. It would need the appropriate review, including any privilege concerns, before that decision.
  8. ESI coordinator: Understood. Locating electronically stored information doesn't itself authorize producing it.
  9. Discovery lawyer: Exactly. Return the collection findings and any unresolved link between the email and attachment.
  10. ESI coordinator: I'll report those limits and request further instructions if the reference cannot be resolved.
Preparing deposition materials without assuming disclosure

Separate fictional litigation exercise: counsel requests a proposed deposition bundle; some selected documents have unresolved review flags.

  1. Associate lawyer: Could you assemble a proposed deposition bundle and identify documents with unresolved review flags?
  2. Litigation paralegal: Several selections still need review. Should I remove the flags to make the bundle easier to read?
  3. Associate lawyer: No. Counsel needs those flags visible before deciding which materials may be used.
  4. Litigation paralegal: I'll separate cleared selections from items awaiting privilege or work-product assessment.
  5. Associate lawyer: Please don't call the second group privileged as a final determination; assessment is pending.
  6. Litigation paralegal: Understood. What timing should I propose for the review conversation?
  7. Associate lawyer: Ask counsel for a slot before the bundle is finalized, without inventing a deadline.
  8. Litigation paralegal: I'll provide the item references and the specific questions needing a decision.
  9. Associate lawyer: Good. The request is for a reviewable proposal, not authorization to disclose every selection.
  10. Litigation paralegal: I'll confirm that scope when I hand over the bundle for discussion.

An exhibit contains an unreviewed attachment

A deposition preparation folder contains an email and a linked attachment. The email has been reviewed, but the attachment has not. The folder is internal; no exhibit release is authorized.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Reviewer: "The attachment remains ___, even though the parent email has been checked."

Answer and explanation

C. unreviewed

Review of one item does not establish that a linked attachment has received the same assessment.

2. Counsel: "Keep the document ___ visible so the relationship is not lost."

Answer and explanation

C. family

The family connects the parent email with its attachment and preserves useful review context.

3. Reviewer: "I will flag the pending question before any exhibit ___."

Answer and explanation

B. release

The case permits internal preparation, not disclosure of unreviewed material as an exhibit.

4. Counsel: "Record my decision in the review ___ before updating the preparation set."

Answer and explanation

B. history

A recorded decision makes the authorization and sequence traceable rather than relying on an informal assumption.

Build vocabulary and collocations — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Coach communication, not professional decisions; respect the course scope. Ask only for fictional or anonymized practice details. Judge clarity, meaning, appropriate tone and the next step. Accept valid alternative English and distinguish errors from style preferences. Do not claim to certify my language level. Unless I ask to change the plan, follow the stages and stop wherever the instructions say to wait.

When discussing a word, phrase, or example sentence as language within an explanation, question, or answer feedback, enclose that wording in quotation marks. For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Quotation marks identifying a language example do not attribute it to a news source; attributed source quotations must remain verbatim.

Practice setting: B2 independent. Use natural professional English with brief explanations. Let me attempt each task without a model first. Offer a hint after difficulty and invite a more precise retry.

Lesson 04: Discovery, ESI, Privilege Review, and Depositions
Original fictional case: Nora is reviewing electronically stored information for a supplier dispute. An email chain discusses commercial terms and includes a lawyer on one message. The chain is in the review set, not the production set. The approved workflow requires uncertain privilege issues to be flagged for Owen, reviewing counsel. A draft production list is due tomorrow, but no release of this chain has been authorized. The team must preserve the original record and explain its current status accurately.
Language workshop: An email chain awaiting a privilege decision
Communication goal: Describe review status and preserve potentially protected material without making a privilege ruling.
Language guidance: Relevance, responsiveness, and privilege answer different questions. Material may respond to a request yet require protection or redaction. A review flag records an unresolved issue; it does not authorize withholding or production on its own.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The chain remains in the review set. / I have flagged a potential privilege issue for counsel. / The copied lawyer's name does not resolve the classification. / Please review the full thread and linked attachments. / Responsiveness and privilege require separate assessments. / This item has not been authorized for production. / The review identifier is R-214; no production number is assigned. / I will update the status after counsel records the decision. / The original record and its relevant metadata remain unchanged. / This list identifies pending review, not final withholding decisions. / Does the protocol require a separate entry for each attachment? / Which passages are approved for redaction in the disclosure copy? / Are you asking whether it was collected or whether it was produced? / The review question remains unresolved ahead of the draft-list deadline. / The witness's recollection and the email record should be identified separately. / Please confirm the authorized production version before release.
Vocabulary: discovery: A process for obtaining relevant information in litigation under applicable rules. / ESI: Electronically stored information, including email and other digital records. / custodian: A person associated with the control or location of relevant records. / collection: Gathering potentially relevant records through an authorized process. / preservation: Maintaining relevant information against inappropriate alteration or loss. / legal hold: Instructions to preserve information for a legal matter. / review set: Documents made available for examination and classification. / production set: Documents selected and prepared for disclosure through an authorized process. / responsiveness: Whether material falls within the scope of a relevant request. / relevance: The relationship of information to an issue in the matter. / privilege review: Assessment of whether a legal protection applies to information. / work product: A protection for specified litigation-preparation material under applicable law. / redaction: Removal or masking of specified content from a disclosure copy. / privilege log: A record describing withheld material as required by applicable procedure. / metadata: Data describing a file, such as dates, authorship, or system attributes. / email thread: Related messages in a continuing email exchange. / attachment family: A parent document and its associated attachments. / deduplication: Identification or removal of duplicate copies in a controlled workflow. / Bates number: A sequential identifier applied to document pages in legal review or production. / clawback: A mechanism for seeking return or protection of inadvertently disclosed material. / deposition: Testimony taken outside trial under applicable procedural rules. / exhibit: Material identified for use in testimony or a proceeding. / transcript: A written record of spoken testimony or proceedings. / review protocol: Instructions governing document assessment and escalation.
Speaking task: Check the answers. Read R-214 as an internal review identifier, not an assigned production reference. Switch roles. Preserve the thread and attachments, flag the potential privilege issue, and keep production unauthorized pending review. Complete the exhibit exchange. Review of the parent email does not establish review or release of its attachment.
Partner: Nora: Document reviewer / Owen: Reviewing counsel
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A deposition preparation folder contains an email and a linked attachment. The email has been reviewed, but the attachment has not. The folder is internal; no exhibit release is authorized.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Nora: A colleague suggested producing now and retrieving it later if necessary. I have not acted on that suggestion because the release decision remains unresolved.
Owen: Do not assume a clawback eliminates every consequence. Continue the approved review and escalate timing concerns instead of relying on a possible later remedy.
Nora: I'll send you R-214 with the attachments and tomorrow's deadline. I'll mark it pending counsel review on the draft list so it doesn't get released accidentally.
Owen: That is a useful handoff. Once I record the decision, update the list and route the correct version through the authorized release process.
END REFERENCE
05Legal Research, Authority, and Memo WritingA persuasive decision described as controlling+

Your goal

Compare authorities and explain a qualified recommendation without overstating precedent.

This lesson in the book, page 40 ↗

A Read the situation

A persuasive decision described as controlling

Jon, an associate, has found a published appellate decision from another jurisdiction supporting a supplier-notice argument. His draft memorandum calls it controlling. Priya, supervising counsel, has asked for the governing forum, relevant statutory text, later treatment, and factual differences to be checked. Those checks are incomplete. The cited case involved written notice; this client used a telephone call. No recommendation has been approved for the client.

Jon: Associate / Priya: Supervising counsel

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is the known source of the decision?

Answer and explanation

D. An appellate court in another jurisdiction

The briefing locates the decision elsewhere; its controlling effect has not been established.

2. Which factual difference is already known?

Answer and explanation

B. Written notice in the decision versus a telephone call here

The notice method differs and may affect whether the decision's reasoning can be applied by analogy.

3. What must happen before the recommendation is approved?

Answer and explanation

B. The requested authority and factual checks

Counsel requested checks of forum, text, treatment, and differences because the preliminary research does not settle the issue.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

A published decision is not automatically binding in another forum. Court hierarchy, jurisdiction, issue, and governing law matter. A database excerpt or summary can locate an issue but should not replace reading the relevant decision and checking its treatment.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
authority
A legal source used to support or govern an analysis.evaluate the cited authority
binding precedent
A prior decision that a court must follow within applicable limits.identify binding precedent
persuasive authority
A source that may influence reasoning without controlling the result.rely on persuasive authority
jurisdiction
A legal territory or scope of a court's authority, depending on context.confirm the relevant jurisdiction
hierarchy
The ordering of courts or sources that affects their relative authority.map the court hierarchy
holding
A court's determination of an issue necessary to its decision.identify the holding
dicta
Judicial observations not necessary to the decision's holding.distinguish dicta from the holding
ratio decidendi
The legal reasoning necessary to a decision in systems using this term.identify the ratio decidendi
statutory text
The wording of an enacted law.examine the statutory text
regulation
A rule issued through an authorized administrative process.check the applicable regulation
legislative history
Materials concerning the development of legislation.assess relevant legislative history
secondary source
Commentary explaining or analyzing law rather than establishing it directly.consult a secondary source
citation
A reference identifying a legal source or passage.verify the citation
pinpoint citation
A reference to the precise location of supporting material.add a pinpoint citation
subsequent treatment
How later authorities have addressed a decision.check subsequent treatment
overruled
Displaced as precedent by an authorized later decision.check whether the decision was overruled
distinguished
Treated as different in a way that limits an earlier decision's application.explain why the case was distinguished
analogous
Similar in legally relevant respects.identify analogous facts
material distinction
A difference that may affect the legal analysis.address a material distinction
procedural posture
The stage and context in which a court decided an issue.compare procedural posture
standard of review
The approach a reviewing court applies to a challenged determination.identify the standard of review
counterargument
A reasoned position against the proposed analysis.address the strongest counterargument
research memorandum
An organized explanation of a legal question, sources, and analysis.revise the research memorandum
synthesis
A combined account of principles drawn from multiple sources.develop a qualified synthesis

Distinguishing a decision does not mean it has been overruled. A holding and dicta have different analytical roles. Preserve the actual basis of the court's decision rather than using every favorable sentence as though it resolved the present issue.

C Notice the language

Strength comes from an accurate limitation

A useful research update identifies the best support and the strongest limitation in the same discussion. A confident voice is compatible with a qualified conclusion. Do not make an authority sound binding merely because it supports the preferred outcome.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Qualify authority
This decision is potentially persuasive; controlling effect is not established.
Identify the forum
We first need to confirm which jurisdiction's law governs this issue.
Locate support
The relevant reasoning appears in the cited passage, not the summary heading.
State a difference
The decision involved written notice; our facts involve a telephone call.
Separate status
The later court distinguished the case rather than overruling it.
Check treatment
I will verify subsequent treatment before relying on the decision.
Frame the recommendation
The argument is available, subject to the governing text and factual distinction.
Close with limits
The memorandum will state both the supporting reasoning and the unresolved checks.
Distinguish reasoning
Is that proposition part of the holding or an observation beyond it?
Avoid a shortcut
Publication alone does not establish binding effect in this forum.
Request precision
Which passage supports that specific proposition?
Compare the stage
The cited decision arose on a different procedural posture.
Preserve an objection
We should address the notice-method distinction rather than omit it.
Explain a secondary source
The commentary helps locate the issue but is not itself the governing enactment.
State an assumption
This section assumes that the identified law governs; that remains to be verified.
Give a bounded update
I have found support for the argument, not a guaranteed outcome.
6 language and precision notes
Controls versus supports
Controls claims governing effect; supports describes assistance to an argument and requires less sweeping authority.
Although clauses
"Although the reasoning helps, the notice method differs" puts support and limitation in a single clear sentence.
On these facts
This phrase confines a proposition to an identified factual setting instead of announcing a universal rule.
By analogy
Explain the relevant similarity and difference when applying reasoning from a different factual situation.
Negative treatment
Name what a later court did; criticized, distinguished, and overruled are not synonyms.
Citation verbs
"The court held" should introduce a holding, while "the court observed" may signal a less central statement.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which wording avoids overstating the decision?

Answer and explanation

B. It may support the argument by analogy, subject to further checks.

The qualified wording preserves both the potential relevance and the incomplete authority checks.

2. Which phrase names later courts' handling of a case?

Answer and explanation

B. subsequent treatment

Subsequent treatment concerns later legal attention to a decision, including limits or changes to its force.

3. Which sentence preserves the known factual difference?

Answer and explanation

A. The cited case used written notice, whereas our client called.

Whereas explicitly contrasts the two known methods without inventing a legal ruling about their significance.

4. Which action best supports a precise source reference?

Answer and explanation

D. Add the page or paragraph supporting the proposition.

A pinpoint citation lets the reviewer inspect the actual supporting passage. A broad citation or a summary does not identify that precise basis.

A persuasive decision described as controlling

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Jon: Associate / Priya: Supervising counsel

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

    I found a published appellate decision supporting our notice argument. My draft says it controls, but I have not finished checking the governing forum or later cases.
  2. Priya
    Change that label for now. It may be 1, but another jurisdiction's published decision does not automatically govern this matter.
  3. Jon

  4. Priya

  5. Jon
    I will retrieve the relevant provision and check which law applies. The commentary I consulted discusses practical notice, but it does not reproduce the complete provision.
  6. Priya

  7. Jon

  8. Priya

  9. Jon

  10. Priya

  13. Jon

  14. Priya
    Good. Record the 7 accurately and verify the citation. The reader needs the actual authority, not a compressed label copied without examination.
  15. Jon
    For the analysis section, I can explain the functional-notice argument and then address the written-versus-oral difference. That gives the reviewing lawyer both sides of the comparison.
  16. Priya

  17. Jon

  18. Priya

Answers and explanations
  1. persuasive authority Turn 2. Persuasive authority may influence the analysis without binding the relevant court; the outstanding forum check prevents a stronger conclusion.
  2. material distinction Turn 4. A material distinction is a difference that could affect the reasoning; the notice method cannot simply be treated as identical.
  3. statutory text Turn 6. Statutory text supplies the enacted wording; commentary can assist research but does not replace checking the provision itself.
  4. holding Turn 8. The holding resolves an issue necessary to the court's decision; a favorable observation may carry a different analytical role.
  5. procedural posture Turn 10. Procedural posture identifies the stage and context of the decision, which can limit what the court actually decided.
  6. distinguished Turn 12. A distinguished case is treated as different in a legally relevant way; that does not itself mean its precedent was overruled.
  7. subsequent treatment Turn 14. Subsequent treatment reports how later authorities handled a decision and helps assess whether reliance remains justified.
  8. counterargument Turn 16. A counterargument identifies a reason against the proposed position; including the known notice-method objection prevents a one-sided recommendation.
  9. pinpoint citation Turn 18. A pinpoint citation identifies the exact supporting location, enabling the reviewer to verify the claim instead of searching an entire decision.
  10. recommendation Turn 20. A recommendation should reflect the support and unresolved limits of the analysis; it is not a guarantee that the argument will succeed.

Dialogue in the book, page 46 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Persuasive does not mean controlling

The lesson's preliminary memo cites a decision from another jurisdiction as controlling; its authority has not been established.

  1. Research assistant: The draft calls this decision controlling, although it came from another jurisdiction.
  2. Research lawyer: Then we need to assess its authority rather than assume it binds the relevant court.
  3. Research assistant: Could you explain binding authority and persuasive authority in plain English?
  4. Research lawyer: Binding authority must be followed when applicable; persuasive authority may inform reasoning without controlling it.
  5. Research assistant: So a useful decision isn't automatically a precedent that controls our issue?
  6. Research lawyer: Correct. Jurisdiction, court hierarchy, and the issue need examination before we characterize its role.
  7. Research assistant: The research is still preliminary. I'll preserve that limitation in the discussion.
  8. Research lawyer: Also consider whether relevant facts or reasoning let us distinguish the case.
  9. Research assistant: I'll describe its possible relevance without presenting the memo's legal conclusion as settled.
  10. Research lawyer: Good. Bring the authority question back for review with the supporting research.
A similar outcome with different facts

Separate fictional research exercise: a located decision reaches a favorable outcome, but its facts differ from the client's account.

  1. Junior lawyer: This decision has the outcome we hope for, so I want to lead with it.
  2. Research supervisor: First explain the factual difference. A favorable result alone doesn't establish a close precedent.
  3. Junior lawyer: Would distinguishing the case mean showing why that difference affects its relevance?
  4. Research supervisor: Yes. Explain the meaningful difference rather than merely listing details that don't matter.
  5. Junior lawyer: We haven't assessed whether the difference is legally significant in this matter.
  6. Research supervisor: Then say so. Don't treat a possible distinction as either decisive or irrelevant yet.
  7. Junior lawyer: Should the memo separately discuss the decision's authority and its factual fit?
  8. Research supervisor: Exactly. Those are related questions, but a strong answer to one doesn't resolve the other.
  9. Junior lawyer: I'll bring both questions to review and avoid describing the outcome as guaranteed.
  10. Research supervisor: That will make the research useful without turning analogy into a promise.
A headnote is not the court's full reasoning

Separate fictional research exercise: an assistant has read a case summary but not the full judgment or its subsequent treatment.

  1. Research assistant: The summary states the principle clearly. Can I cite that as the court's complete reasoning?
  2. Research lawyer: Not yet. A summary helps locate an issue, but it doesn't replace reviewing the decision.
  3. Research assistant: So the summary is a research aid, while the judgment supplies the reasoning to examine?
  4. Research lawyer: Correct. We also haven't checked the decision's subsequent treatment or its authority here.
  5. Research assistant: Would calling it binding authority now combine several questions we haven't answered?
  6. Research lawyer: Yes. We need to assess the source, relevant proposition, and applicable authority separately.
  7. Research assistant: I'll locate the judgment and keep the current note labeled preliminary research.
  8. Research lawyer: Please identify the actual passage supporting the proposition rather than copying the summary alone.
  9. Research assistant: Then I'll ask for review of its relevance and any limits before relying on it.
  10. Research lawyer: Good. Clear source distinctions are more useful than an unsupported authoritative label.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

A persuasive decision described as controlling
  1. Check the dialogue. Contrast another jurisdiction's decision and written notice with this client's telephone call.
  2. Switch roles. Retain the forum, governing-text and later-treatment checks; say persuasive support rather than established controlling authority.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A summary article is not the regulation

An assistant finds a trade article saying a regulatory exception applies broadly. The team has not checked the current regulation, defined terms, or amendments. Counsel has requested the underlying sources.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Assistant: "The article is a ___ source, not the governing regulation."

Answer and explanation

B. secondary

Commentary explains a rule but does not itself establish the enacted or issued requirements.

2. Counsel: "Retrieve the current ___ and relevant definitions."

Answer and explanation

B. text

The wording and definitions are needed to assess the actual scope rather than rely on a summary.

3. Assistant: "I will flag the claimed exception as ___ until that review."

Answer and explanation

A. unverified

The trade article alone does not establish whether the exception applies to the present facts.

4. Counsel: "Keep the source references attached to the research ___."

Answer and explanation

A. memorandum

The memorandum should allow a reviewer to trace and check the analysis against its underlying sources.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Course: Law English
Professional audience: lawyers, paralegals, compliance staff, contracts specialists, legal operations teams, and law-adjacent professionals
Scope: Fictional language practice, not legal advice or qualification to practice law. Terminology, duties, privilege, deadlines, and procedure depend on jurisdiction and facts. Lesson 05: Legal Research, Authority, and Memo Writing
Original fictional case: Jon, an associate, has found a published appellate decision from another jurisdiction supporting a supplier-notice argument. His draft memorandum calls it controlling. Priya, supervising counsel, has asked for the governing forum, relevant statutory text, later treatment, and factual differences to be checked. Those checks are incomplete. The cited case involved written notice; this client used a telephone call. No recommendation has been approved for the client.
Language workshop: A persuasive decision described as controlling
Communication goal: Compare authorities and explain a qualified recommendation without overstating precedent.
Language guidance: A published decision is not automatically binding in another forum. Court hierarchy, jurisdiction, issue, and governing law matter. A database excerpt or summary can locate an issue but should not replace reading the relevant decision and checking its treatment.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): This decision is potentially persuasive; controlling effect is not established. / We first need to confirm which jurisdiction's law governs this issue. / The relevant reasoning appears in the cited passage, not the summary heading. / The decision involved written notice; our facts involve a telephone call. / The later court distinguished the case rather than overruling it. / I will verify subsequent treatment before relying on the decision. / The argument is available, subject to the governing text and factual distinction. / The memorandum will state both the supporting reasoning and the unresolved checks. / Is that proposition part of the holding or an observation beyond it? / Publication alone does not establish binding effect in this forum. / Which passage supports that specific proposition? / The cited decision arose on a different procedural posture. / We should address the notice-method distinction rather than omit it. / The commentary helps locate the issue but is not itself the governing enactment. / This section assumes that the identified law governs; that remains to be verified. / I have found support for the argument, not a guaranteed outcome.
Vocabulary: authority: A legal source used to support or govern an analysis. / binding precedent: A prior decision that a court must follow within applicable limits. / persuasive authority: A source that may influence reasoning without controlling the result. / jurisdiction: A legal territory or scope of a court's authority, depending on context. / hierarchy: The ordering of courts or sources that affects their relative authority. / holding: A court's determination of an issue necessary to its decision. / dicta: Judicial observations not necessary to the decision's holding. / ratio decidendi: The legal reasoning necessary to a decision in systems using this term. / statutory text: The wording of an enacted law. / regulation: A rule issued through an authorized administrative process. / legislative history: Materials concerning the development of legislation. / secondary source: Commentary explaining or analyzing law rather than establishing it directly. / citation: A reference identifying a legal source or passage. / pinpoint citation: A reference to the precise location of supporting material. / subsequent treatment: How later authorities have addressed a decision. / overruled: Displaced as precedent by an authorized later decision. / distinguished: Treated as different in a way that limits an earlier decision's application. / analogous: Similar in legally relevant respects. / material distinction: A difference that may affect the legal analysis. / procedural posture: The stage and context in which a court decided an issue. / standard of review: The approach a reviewing court applies to a challenged determination. / counterargument: A reasoned position against the proposed analysis. / research memorandum: An organized explanation of a legal question, sources, and analysis. / synthesis: A combined account of principles drawn from multiple sources.
Speaking task: Check the dialogue. Contrast another jurisdiction's decision and written notice with this client's telephone call. Switch roles. Retain the forum, governing-text and later-treatment checks; say persuasive support rather than established controlling authority. Complete the article exchange. Request the current regulation and definitions, keeping the claimed exception unverified.
Partner: Jon: Associate / Priya: Supervising counsel
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: An assistant finds a trade article saying a regulatory exception applies broadly. The team has not checked the current regulation, defined terms, or amendments. Counsel has requested the underlying sources.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Jon: I will also replace the broad citation with the specific paragraph supporting the proposition. That should make it easier to check whether my summary is faithful.
Priya: A pinpoint citation helps. Keep the quotation brief and make your own reasoning explicit; the passage should support the analysis rather than stand in for it.
Jon: I'll call it a potentially useful analogy and flag the notice-method difference. Can we discuss the recommendation after I finish the governing-law and treatment checks?
Priya: That is an appropriately bounded recommendation. Send the revised memorandum with the outstanding checks clearly identified before anything goes to the client.
END REFERENCE

06Contracts, Redlines, and NegotiationChanging delivery time without conceding the whole clause+

Your goal

Propose a precise amendment, preserve linked terms, and distinguish a negotiating position from acceptance.

This lesson in the book, page 49 ↗

A Read the situation

Changing delivery time without conceding the whole clause

A draft services agreement requires delivery within ten days after a purchase order. Operations needs fifteen business days after receipt of complete specifications. The draft does not define business day or explain incomplete specifications. Elena, commercial counsel, and Marcus, operations director, are preparing a proposed redline. The customer has not accepted any change, and neither participant has approval to concede remedies or liability limits. Their task is to define the proposed timing change and identify related questions for review.

Marcus: Operations director / Elena: Commercial counsel

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What timing does operations need?

Answer and explanation

A. Fifteen business days after complete specifications are received

The briefing specifies both a business-day period and receipt of complete specifications as its proposed starting event.

2. What has the customer accepted?

Answer and explanation

C. No change yet

The proposed changes are still being prepared and the customer has not accepted them.

3. What falls outside the participants' current approval?

Answer and explanation

C. Conceding remedies or liability limits

Their authority covers preparation and review, not the stated concessions on remedies or liability.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Ten days after a purchase order and fifteen business days after complete specifications differ in both duration and trigger. Replacing only the numeral leaves the operational problem unresolved. The relevant calendar and completion standard also need clear drafting.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
redline
A version showing proposed changes to existing wording.circulate a proposed redline
markup
Edits or comments displayed on a draft document.reconcile competing markups
operative clause
Wording that establishes a substantive term or obligation.revise the operative clause
defined term
A word or phrase assigned a specified meaning in a document.use the defined term consistently
business day
A working day as defined by the relevant agreement or rule.clarify the business-day definition
trigger event
The occurrence that starts an obligation or time period.identify the trigger event
condition precedent
An event that must occur before a specified duty or effect arises.review the proposed condition precedent
covenant
A contractual promise to do or refrain from doing something.assess the covenant wording
representation
A statement of fact with legal significance in context.qualify the representation
warranty
A contractual assurance whose effect depends on its terms and governing law.review the warranty scope
indemnity
An obligation to bear specified losses or liabilities under agreed terms.negotiate the indemnity provision
limitation of liability
A clause restricting specified liability under defined conditions.preserve the limitation of liability
liability cap
A stated upper limit on specified liability.verify the liability cap
carve-out
An exception to a provision's general scope.define the carve-out narrowly
cure period
Time allowed to remedy a specified failure.negotiate the cure period
termination right
A contractual ability to end an agreement under stated conditions.clarify the termination right
notice provision
Terms governing how required notices are given.follow the notice provision
order of precedence
A rule for resolving conflicts among contract documents.check the order of precedence
entire agreement clause
A clause addressing which materials comprise the parties' agreement.review the entire agreement clause
amendment mechanism
The required process for changing an agreement.follow the amendment mechanism
effective date
The date from which an agreement or change has stated effect.confirm the effective date
execution copy
A version prepared for signing after the required review.verify the execution copy
fallback position
An alternative negotiating position available within authority.confirm the approved fallback position
reservation of rights
A statement intended to preserve identified rights or positions.review the reservation of rights

A proposed redline is not an execution copy. A commercial concession on timing does not automatically approve a change to remedies, indemnity, or liability. Authority, agreement, and formal amendment requirements must be checked separately.

C Notice the language

Negotiate the variable, not an undefined package

A conversational "that works" may hide different assumptions about the clock, trigger, or scope of agreement. Restate the exact proposed term and identify what remains unchanged or unresolved. A redline is a proposal until the relevant approvals and agreement are established.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
State the requirement
Operations needs fifteen business days after receipt of complete specifications.
Identify both changes
We are proposing a different period and a different starting event.
Clarify the definition
Which calendar does the business-day definition use?
Limit the proposal
This markup addresses delivery timing, not the liability allocation.
Preserve status
The proposed wording remains subject to approval and customer agreement.
Check completeness
We need an objective way to identify the required specifications.
Separate concessions
No change to remedies has been authorized.
Close with a redline
I will circulate the marked clause and list the linked provisions for review.
Avoid ambiguity
Does "received" mean received through the agreed submission channel?
Explain the dependency
We cannot start the production clock without the specified inputs.
Request a fallback
Which alternative timing position has the business approved?
Check interaction
Does the purchase order conflict with the main agreement?
Preserve a limit
Please keep the unresolved calendar definition visible in the comments.
Confirm the version
Is this the approved execution copy or an earlier negotiating draft?
Reject implied acceptance
Preparing the change does not establish customer acceptance.
Make a bounded commitment
I can confirm the proposed wording, not promise that it will be accepted.
6 language and precision notes
Within versus after
Within sets a deadline relative to a trigger; after names the trigger relationship without necessarily defining the endpoint alone.
Calendar qualification
State calendar or business days when the distinction matters, and check the agreement's definition.
Subject to approval
Attach this phrase to the proposal so internal readiness cannot be mistaken for authorized acceptance.
Without changing
Use this phrase to limit a revision's intended scope, but still inspect linked clauses for unintended effects.
Proposal verbs
Propose and request are different from agree and accept; the verb should match the negotiating stage.
Version language
Draft, redline, clean copy, and execution copy identify document states, not interchangeable file descriptions.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which proposal captures operations' stated need?

Answer and explanation

B. Fifteen business days after receipt of complete specifications

The correct proposal preserves both the required duration and the new triggering event.

2. Which sentence accurately describes authority?

Answer and explanation

B. We can propose timing changes, but no remedy concession is approved.

The briefing permits preparation of a timing proposal while expressly withholding authority for remedy concessions.

3. Which phrase identifies competing document priority?

Answer and explanation

A. order of precedence

An order of precedence addresses conflicts between documents. Governing law, notices and liability allocation address other contractual questions.

4. Which status statement is appropriate before customer agreement?

Answer and explanation

C. The redline is a proposal subject to approval and agreement.

A draft redline records a proposed change, not acceptance or completion of signing.

Check explanations in the book, page 95 ↗

E Conversations

Changing delivery time without conceding the whole clause

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Marcus: Operations director / Elena: Commercial counsel

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • execution copy
  • fallback position
  • propose
  • defined term
  • order of precedence
  • concession
  • redline
  • business day
  • scope
  • trigger event
  1. Marcus
    The draft starts ten days at the purchase order. We need fifteen business days after complete specifications arrive. Changing the number alone won't solve it.
  2. Elena
    Agreed. The 1 needs to show both changes. We'll keep them visible instead of presenting this as a simple five-day extension.
  3. Marcus
    An order can arrive without the dimensions. Under the present wording the clock would run even though the inputs needed for production are missing.
  4. Elena
    Then receipt of complete specifications is the proposed 2. The order alone doesn't start that proposed clock unless the required specifications have actually been received.
  5. Marcus
    I'll list the required inputs in a schedule. Can we use that same list wherever the agreement refers to complete specifications?
  6. Elena
    Yes. A consistent 3 will help connect the schedule and operative clause. We still need to check how completeness and receipt will be identified.
  7. Marcus
    The customer and our production team use different holiday calendars. Fifteen working days may end on different dates depending on which calendar they mean.
  8. Elena
    That's why the 4 definition needs agreement. Don't leave the relevant weekends and holidays to assumption.
  9. Marcus
    Procurement may ask for a shorter cure period in return. Can I offer that now to make the delivery proposal easier to accept?
  10. Elena
    No such 5 is authorized. A remedy change needs its own review; it isn't included merely because we're discussing delivery timing.
  11. Marcus
    Then I need instructions on alternatives before the call. Otherwise I could agree to something the business hasn't assessed.
  12. Elena
    Correct. Request an approved 6. Until then, explain the timing requirement without inventing another concession.
  13. Marcus
    The purchase order template also carries ten days. Updating the main agreement could leave two competing delivery clauses in circulation.
  14. Elena
    Flag that conflict and the 7 provision. We should reconcile the documents, not assume the customer will choose our preferred wording.
  15. Marcus
    For today's message, can I say the new timing is agreed internally, or would that blur the status before approval?
  16. Elena
    Say we 8 fifteen business days after complete specifications, subject to approval and customer agreement. That states the request without implying a completed amendment.
  17. Marcus
    There are two marked versions. Once wording is approved and accepted, we'll need to confirm which changes belong in the signing version.
  18. Elena
    Yes. Reconcile them before preparing the 9. Removing visible markup doesn't itself establish that every term is approved.
  19. Marcus
    I'll send the input schedule, calendar question and template conflict with the proposed clause. No remedy or liability change will be included.
  20. Elena
    That keeps the 10 clear. We can review a defined timing proposal instead of discovering unrelated concessions inside the clean document.

Answers and explanations
  1. redline Turn 2. A redline shows proposed wording changes, here to both the period and its starting event.
  2. trigger event Turn 4. The proposed trigger is actual receipt of complete specifications; receipt of an order without those specifications does not start that proposed period.
  3. defined term Turn 6. A defined term assigns a specific meaning, allowing the schedule and clause to use one completion standard.
  4. business day Turn 8. Business day needs a relevant definition; the parties cannot assume that different working calendars are identical.
  5. concession Turn 10. A concession gives negotiating ground; changing the cure period could affect remedies beyond the authorized proposal.
  6. fallback position Turn 12. A fallback position is a negotiating alternative that needs authorization, not an improvised concession.
  7. order of precedence Turn 14. The order of precedence addresses conflicting documents; the inconsistent purchase order template still needs review.
  8. propose Turn 16. Propose identifies suggested wording, not completed approval or customer agreement to a change.
  9. execution copy Turn 18. An execution copy is prepared for signing after review; clean appearance alone does not establish approval.
  10. scope Turn 20. Scope defines what the change covers, separating authorized timing revisions from unapproved remedy concessions.

Dialogue in the book, page 55 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Proposing fifteen days without announcing agreement

The lesson's services draft says ten days; the commercial team needs fifteen. Wording remains subject to legal and counterparty review.

  1. Commercial manager: The draft requires delivery within ten days, but our team needs fifteen.
  2. Contract lawyer: We can propose a redline, provided it is clear that the change requires review and agreement.
  3. Commercial manager: Could you tell the customer that fifteen days is now the contractual commitment?
  4. Contract lawyer: Not before agreement. Our proposal doesn't amend the draft merely because we prefer it.
  5. Commercial manager: Should we also check whether delivery wording affects any related warranty provision?
  6. Contract lawyer: Yes. Connected terms need review rather than an isolated number change.
  7. Commercial manager: I can explain the operational requirement, but I can't approve the legal wording.
  8. Contract lawyer: Then bring that requirement into the negotiation and leave the drafting decision with the review team.
  9. Commercial manager: I'll present fifteen days as our requested timing, not as an accepted term.
  10. Contract lawyer: For review, I propose replacing 'within ten days' with 'within fifteen days', leaving the existing timing trigger and other wording unchanged. This remains subject to legal review and counterparty agreement.
Scope reduction instead of an unsupported warranty

Separate fictional contract negotiation: a customer requests support for all equipment, while the supplier's proposal covers one named product line.

  1. Customer procurement lead: Could the warranty cover all our equipment, not only the named product line?
  2. Supplier contract manager: That's broader than the proposal. We can assess it, but cannot confirm coverage today.
  3. Customer procurement lead: Would keeping the current price be possible if we narrowed the request?
  4. Supplier contract manager: We can take a defined scope for review; pricing and warranty wording remain unapproved.
  5. Customer procurement lead: Then let's compare the named product line with a separately assessed expansion.
  6. Supplier contract manager: Agreed. We should also check related representations rather than promise capabilities we haven't verified.
  7. Customer procurement lead: I can identify the equipment list, but I won't describe expanded coverage as agreed.
  8. Supplier contract manager: Please do. That will make the review concrete without changing the current proposal silently.
  9. Customer procurement lead: We'll return to price after the scope and proposed terms have been assessed.
  10. Supplier contract manager: Good. For now, both the expansion and its conditions remain open.
A liability request needs coordinated review

Separate fictional contract exercise: procurement requests a broader indemnity while the draft's limitation-of-liability section is still under review.

  1. Procurement manager: Can we accept the broader indemnity today and discuss the liability limit later?
  2. Contract counsel: Those provisions may interact. We should review them together before confirming acceptance.
  3. Procurement manager: I'm trying to keep negotiations moving. What can I offer as a practical next step?
  4. Contract counsel: Offer a coordinated review of the requested indemnity and the limitation-of-liability wording.
  5. Procurement manager: Could I say the business accepts the concept, subject to wording?
  6. Contract counsel: Only if that accurately reflects authorized instructions. We haven't established such acceptance here.
  7. Procurement manager: Then I'll say we are evaluating the request and ask for the counterparty's priority.
  8. Contract counsel: That preserves room for negotiation without inventing approval or explaining a legal effect prematurely.
  9. Procurement manager: I'll bring their response and the linked clauses to the review discussion.
  10. Contract counsel: Good. We can then formulate a conditional proposal grounded in the actual instructions.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

Changing delivery time without conceding the whole clause
  1. Check the answers. Read both proposed changes: fifteen business days and receipt of complete specifications, not just a replacement numeral.
  2. Switch roles. Name the missing calendar definition and purchase-order conflict; do not add an unauthorized remedy concession.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A renewal date changes, but termination language does not

A team is authorized to propose a new renewal date. The notice period and termination rights remain under separate review. The counterparty has not accepted the date change.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Commercial lead: "Our ___ changes the renewal date only."

Answer and explanation

C. proposal

Proposal identifies negotiating status and limits the requested change to the authorized date issue.

2. Counsel: "Keep the separate notice-period question ___ in the review note."

Answer and explanation

A. unresolved

The notice period remains under review and should not appear settled merely because a date is proposed.

3. Commercial lead: "No change to termination rights is currently ___."

Answer and explanation

B. authorized

The facts do not grant authority to concede termination rights as part of the date discussion.

4. Counsel: "Confirm the accepted wording before preparing the execution ___."

Answer and explanation

C. copy

The signing version should reflect approved and accepted wording rather than an unresolved negotiation draft.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Lesson 06: Contracts, Redlines, and Negotiation
Original fictional case: A draft services agreement requires delivery within ten days after a purchase order. Operations needs fifteen business days after receipt of complete specifications. The draft does not define business day or explain incomplete specifications. Elena, commercial counsel, and Marcus, operations director, are preparing a proposed redline. The customer has not accepted any change, and neither participant has approval to concede remedies or liability limits. Their task is to define the proposed timing change and identify related questions for review.
Language workshop: Changing delivery time without conceding the whole clause
Communication goal: Propose a precise amendment, preserve linked terms, and distinguish a negotiating position from acceptance.
Language guidance: Ten days after a purchase order and fifteen business days after complete specifications differ in both duration and trigger. Replacing only the numeral leaves the operational problem unresolved. The relevant calendar and completion standard also need clear drafting.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Operations needs fifteen business days after receipt of complete specifications. / We are proposing a different period and a different starting event. / Which calendar does the business-day definition use? / This markup addresses delivery timing, not the liability allocation. / The proposed wording remains subject to approval and customer agreement. / We need an objective way to identify the required specifications. / No change to remedies has been authorized. / I will circulate the marked clause and list the linked provisions for review. / Does "received" mean received through the agreed submission channel? / We cannot start the production clock without the specified inputs. / Which alternative timing position has the business approved? / Does the purchase order conflict with the main agreement? / Please keep the unresolved calendar definition visible in the comments. / Is this the approved execution copy or an earlier negotiating draft? / Preparing the change does not establish customer acceptance. / I can confirm the proposed wording, not promise that it will be accepted.
Vocabulary: redline: A version showing proposed changes to existing wording. / markup: Edits or comments displayed on a draft document. / operative clause: Wording that establishes a substantive term or obligation. / defined term: A word or phrase assigned a specified meaning in a document. / business day: A working day as defined by the relevant agreement or rule. / trigger event: The occurrence that starts an obligation or time period. / condition precedent: An event that must occur before a specified duty or effect arises. / covenant: A contractual promise to do or refrain from doing something. / representation: A statement of fact with legal significance in context. / warranty: A contractual assurance whose effect depends on its terms and governing law. / indemnity: An obligation to bear specified losses or liabilities under agreed terms. / limitation of liability: A clause restricting specified liability under defined conditions. / liability cap: A stated upper limit on specified liability. / carve-out: An exception to a provision's general scope. / cure period: Time allowed to remedy a specified failure. / termination right: A contractual ability to end an agreement under stated conditions. / notice provision: Terms governing how required notices are given. / order of precedence: A rule for resolving conflicts among contract documents. / entire agreement clause: A clause addressing which materials comprise the parties' agreement. / amendment mechanism: The required process for changing an agreement. / effective date: The date from which an agreement or change has stated effect. / execution copy: A version prepared for signing after the required review. / fallback position: An alternative negotiating position available within authority. / reservation of rights: A statement intended to preserve identified rights or positions.
Speaking task: Check the answers. Read both proposed changes: fifteen business days and receipt of complete specifications, not just a replacement numeral. Switch roles. Name the missing calendar definition and purchase-order conflict; do not add an unauthorized remedy concession. Complete the renewal exchange. Keep the notice period unresolved and termination rights outside the approved date proposal.

Marcus: I'll send the input schedule, calendar question and template conflict with the proposed clause. No remedy or liability change will be included.
Elena: That keeps the scope clear. We can review a defined timing proposal instead of discovering unrelated concessions inside the clean document.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.
